title: Simple Financial Management in Housewife Communities: A Qualitative Study on Daily Financial Management Patterns
venue: International Journal of Applied Economics, Accounting and Management (IJAEAM)
tldr: A qualitative case study of 25 Indonesian housewives revealed sophisticated informal financial ecosystems including ROSCAs, mental accounting, and community risk-sharing mechanisms that challenge narratives of financial vulnerability and demonstrate remarkable economic agency within resource constraints.
problem_and_motivation: Indonesian housewives are primary household financial managers yet have lower financial literacy rates (36.1%) than men (40.6%) per OJK data. Despite managing complex daily finances, their practices remain largely invisible in economic calculations and formal financial education. The study addresses the gap in understanding daily financial management patterns in resource-constrained communities.
approach: Qualitative case study with 25 housewives in Salatiga, Central Java. Data collection: in-depth interviews (60-90 min each), non-participant observation of community financial activities, and document analysis over July-August 2024. Analysis used ATLAS.ti with open, axial, and selective coding. Triangulation enhanced validity. Member checking with participants confirmed accuracy of interpretations.
findings: Housewives developed sophisticated financial practices including: (1) recording systems ranging from simple books to mental accounting with envelope segregation; (2) expenditure prioritization into primary/secondary/tertiary needs; (3) adaptive strategies including income diversification, ROSCAs (arisan), jimpitan (microsavings), collective buying, and food substitution; (4) micro-scale emergency funds and social support networks; (5) community serves as informal financial institution providing knowledge transfer, collective norms, and mediation to formal systems. Gender dynamics create 'bounded authority' where women exercise agency within constrained domains.
definitions: ROSCAs (Arisan): Rotating Savings and Credit Associations serving as forced savings and community lending mechanisms
Jimpitan: Community-based daily microsavings of rice or small change for collective social funds
Mental Accounting: Cognitive budgeting heuristics where money is categorized by purpose regardless of physical location
Bounded Authority: Concept describing women's significant financial responsibility without commensurate decision-making power
Shadow Banking: Informal community financial systems that function as alternatives to formal banking (Rutherford)
citations: Joo (1998) - Conceptual Model of Personal Financial Wellness
Kabeer - Bounded power concept for women's economic agency
Rutherford - Shadow banking concept for informal financial systems
OJK (Financial Services Authority) - Indonesian financial literacy data
Rahmatia et al. - Community-centered financial education approaches

topic_relevance.mapping_rationale: Core focus on financial literacy levels and informal financial knowledge transfer within housewife communities
Explores detailed financial management patterns, recording practices, expenditure prioritization, and saving behaviors
Examines how housewives allocate income across primary/secondary/tertiary needs and manage daily liquidity

limitations: Small sample size (25 participants) in one city limits generalizability
Qualitative design provides depth but not statistical breadth
Focus on housewives only; does not capture male financial perspectives
Short two-month fieldwork period may miss seasonal variations
Cultural specificity of Javanese context may not generalize to other Indonesian regions
remember_this: Housewife communities develop sophisticated informal financial systems (ROSCAs, jimpitan, mental accounting) that function as parallel financial institutions. Women demonstrate 'bounded authority'—significant operational control over daily finances without commensurate decision-making power over major financial decisions. Community serves as knowledge transfer mechanism, norm formation space, and bridge to formal financial systems.
